title: Open ranges on a toy graph
prompt: Here's a toy version of the graph as five small frozen dataclasses: Range(name, bound), Const(value), Add(a, b), Store(offset, value) and End(effect, range), where End closes the range it names. Write opens(n: Node) -> list[str]: the names of the ranges n depends on that no End has closed, sorted, with no duplicates. This is the property your compiler computes for every UOp.

tests.expr: (lambda i, j: opens(Store(Add(i, j), Const(0))))(Range('i', 2), Range('j', 3))
(lambda i, j: opens(End(Store(Add(i, j), Const(0)), j)))(Range('i', 2), Range('j', 3))
(lambda i, j: opens(End(End(Store(Add(i, j), Const(0)), j), i)))(Range('i', 2), Range('j', 3))
(lambda i, j: opens(Add(j, Add(i, j))))(Range('i', 2), Range('j', 3))

hints: A Range is open in itself. A Const has nothing open. Add and Store take the union of their children.
End(e, r) is the one exception: the opens of e, minus the name of r.
A match statement with class patterns like case Range(name, _): reads each case off the node. sorted(set(a) | set(b)) keeps the result sorted and free of duplicates.
explain: Open ranges are a union over sources, with Range adding its own name and End removing the range it closes. Sorting a set keeps the result canonical. The nodes are frozen dataclasses, so they hash, and the real compiler can memoize this per node with a dict, because shared subgraphs would otherwise be walked many times.
